title: The Hymn of Philip K. Dick (ASE Conference Talk)
author: Erik Davis
card_summary: Erik Davis's conference talk for the Association for the Study of Esotericism (ASE) on PKD's use of the Gnostic Hymn of the Pearl. Traces PKD's textual engagement with the Hymn (sourced via Encyclopedia Britannica and Hans Jonas's Gnostic Religion) from the February 1975 letter to Claudia Bush through the late Exegesis folders, where PKD attaches the salvator salvandus (redeemed redeemer) figure to VALIS itself.
page_summary:
Erik Davis's ASE (Association for the Study of Esotericism) conference talk 'The Hymn of Philip K. Dick' is a focused study of PKD's reading and re-deployment of one specific Gnostic text — the 'Hymn of the Pearl' embedded in the third-century Acts of Thomas. Davis tracks PKD's engagement with the Hymn from the February 16, 1975 letter to Claudia Bush (where PKD quotes the Encyclopedia Britannica's 15th-edition account of the text) through the late Exegesis folders (where PKD attaches the salvator salvandus / 'redeemed redeemer' figure derived from the Hymn to VALIS itself). The piece is short, scholarly-precise about sources, and one of the more disciplined examples of Davis's approach to PKD: comparative-religious without flattening into either pop-Gnosticism or skeptical reduction.

Argument: PKD reaches for the Hymn of the Pearl as a narrative framework that helps construct the 2-3-74 events as a possible meaning of his own illegible experience. The text — a fairy-tale allegory of spiritual awakening, recall, and rescue — gives PKD a structure within which the fish-sign / pink-beam encounter can be read as recognition of celestial origin, with the delivery-woman figure functioning as messenger and the messenger-redeemer trope (the salvator salvandus, 'redeemed redeemer,' sourced from Manichaean material via Jonas) eventually identified with VALIS itself. Davis draws on the recursive structure of the salvator salvandus to explain why PKD found the Hymn so compelling: it matched the aporias of self-reference and paradox already operative in the fiction.

Key quoted passages: PKD to Bush, February 16, 1975 (the Britannica quotation and the 'beauty of this text' remark); PKD to Le Guin, September 23, 1974 (the original ixthys / pharmacy / pink beam narrative and the 'disinhibiting stimuli' GABA hypothesis); the Sutin-In Pursuit of VALIS excerpt on the fish sign as Gnostic reminder of celestial origins; the late Exegesis entry equating VALIS with the salvator salvandus and with the Gnostic Christ.

Contributions to PKD studies: (1) the most disciplined source-tracking of PKD's specific Gnostic engagements via Britannica and Hans Jonas; (2) the centrality of the Hymn of the Pearl as PKD's first and most enduring Gnostic narrative framework; (3) the salvator salvandus reading of VALIS as recursive redeemer-figure; (4) the model of PKD as 'a passive relay node in a salvational network' — a frame for the Exegesis's apostolic self-presentation that avoids both inflation and dismissal.

Position in the literature: Davis works in the comparative-religious lineage shared with Jeffrey Kripal and the post-2011 Exegesis annotators (Davis was himself one of the rotating annotators on the Lethem/Jackson edition). Lorenzo DiTommaso's 2001 SFS article 'Gnosticism and Dualism in the Early Fiction of Philip K. Dick' provides the philological-historical anchor against which Davis's source-tracking can be checked. Gabriel McKee's Pink Beams of Light from the God in the Gutter (2004) is the parallel theological monograph treatment.
